flawed_step: Step 4: the claim that a longest cycle C in a 3-connected claw-free graph must contain every vertex. Neither 3-connectivity nor claw-freeness forces this. The inflated Petersen graph (every vertex replaced by a triangle) is 3-connected and claw-free but has no Hamiltonian cycle.
counterexample: Let P be the Petersen graph and let T(P) be the graph made by replacing each vertex of P with a triangle, so each triangle vertex takes one of the original three edges. T(P) has 30 vertices and every vertex has degree 3. It is claw-free because every vertex's neighbourhood contains an adjacent pair (its two triangle-mates). It is 3-connected: a vertex or edge cut of size at most 2 would give an edge cut of size at most 2 in P, and P is 3-edge-connected. For cubic graphs, vertex and edge connectivity are equal. T(P) is the line graph of the subdivision S(P). A Hamiltonian cycle in T(P) would give a closed trail in S(P) that touches every edge. Since S(P) has maximum degree 3, that trail is a cycle, and it would have to be a Hamiltonian cycle of P. P has none, so T(P) is not Hamiltonian.
assessment_summary:
Proof attempt:
1. Let G be 3-connected and claw-free. G has at least 4 vertices and minimum degree at least 3, so it contains a cycle. Justified.
2. Take a longest cycle C in G. Justified, since G is finite.
3. Suppose some vertex v is not on C. By 3-connectivity (Menger/fan lemma), there are 3 paths from v to C that share only v. Justified.
4. Using claw-freeness at the ends of those paths on C, try to reroute C through v and get a longer cycle, so that C must contain every vertex. NOT justified. Claw-freeness only says that among the three neighbours of a vertex on C, two are adjacent. This does not give a longer cycle; the known local arguments need stronger hypotheses. The Matthews–Sumner conjecture, which asks this for 4-connected claw-free graphs, is still open. For 3-connected graphs the step is actually false: in the inflated Petersen graph T(P), no cycle covers every vertex.
5. Conclude that C is Hamiltonian. Not justified, because it depends on step 4.
Checking the counterexample:
(a) T(P) is cubic and claw-free, because each neighbourhood contains an edge of a triangle. Justified.
(b) T(P) is 3-connected. A 2-edge cut must either split a triangle, which uses both cut edges and leaves the separated vertex still attached through its outside edge, or come from a ≤2-edge cut in P, which does not exist. For cubic graphs, vertex connectivity equals edge connectivity. Justified.
(c) T(P) is the line graph of S(P), so a Hamiltonian cycle in T(P) is the same as a closed trail in S(P) that touches every edge. Harary–Nash-Williams theorem. Justified.
(d) Because S(P) has maximum degree 3, that trail is a cycle, which is a cycle D in P. Every edge of P not on D needs both ends on D. Any vertex of P off D would have all its edges off D, which forces it onto D, a contradiction. So D is a Hamiltonian cycle of P, and P has none. Justified.
The statement is false.
